title: Review: Enzymes and metabolism
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for IB Diploma Biology (review status in the bank: ai-specialist-reviewed-gate-verified-2026-09-21-awaiting-human-signoff). Questions: C1.1#q01, C1.1#q04, C1.1#q05, C1.1#q08, C1.1#q09, C1.1#q10, C1.1#q13, C1.1#q16, C1.1#q18, C1.1#q02, C1.1#q03, C1.1#q11. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Active site
items.clue: The region of an enzyme to which the substrate binds and where catalysis occurs.

items.label: Immobilized enzyme
items.clue: An enzyme held in a fixed position, for example by being embedded in a membrane.

items.label: Enzyme-substrate specificity
items.clue: The property that each enzyme catalyses only one reaction or one type of reaction.

items.label: Hydrolysis
items.clue: A reaction in which a covalent bond within a molecule is broken by the addition of a water molecule.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how an enzyme acts as a catalyst in a cell?

options.text: It increases the rate of a reaction that could occur without it, and is released unchanged.
It is converted into product along with the substrate, so the cell must keep making it.
It makes possible a reaction that could not take place at all in its absence in the cell.
It transfers energy to the substrate so that the reaction is driven forward faster.

questions.stem: A yeast cell synthesizes one amino acid through a pathway of several steps. Why does this pathway require several different enzymes rather than one?

options.text: One enzyme could catalyse every step if the substrates were supplied in the correct order.
Each step needs a different amount of energy, and each enzyme supplies a fixed amount of energy.
Enzymes are used up as they work, so several are needed to complete all the steps.
Each step has a different substrate, and an active site fits only one substrate.

questions.stem: Which process is an example of anabolism?

options.text: The formation of glycogen from glucose monomers by condensation reactions
The oxidation of glucose in cell respiration to provide ATP for the cell
The digestion of starch in the gut into maltose and then glucose
The hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate, which releases energy

questions.explanation: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones; the formation of macromolecules such as glycogen from monomers by condensation is one of the guide's named examples, along with protein synthesis and photosynthesis.

questions.stem: According to the induced-fit model, what happens when a substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme?

options.text: The rigid active site admits only an exactly matching substrate.
The active site closes around a substrate that keeps its shape.
The enzyme seizes the substrate and holds it without any changes.
Both the enzyme and the substrate change shape as they bind.

questions.explanation: Students should recognize that both substrate and enzyme change shape when binding occurs. The closer fit strains bonds within the substrate, which is part of how catalysis is achieved.

questions.stem: ATP synthase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and cannot move freely. How do its substrates, ADP and phosphate, reach its active site?

options.text: They move by random molecular motion in the fluid and collide with the fixed active site.
They cannot, so an enzyme fixed in a membrane works only after being released from it.
The enzyme extends its active site out into the fluid to capture passing substrates.
They are carried to the enzyme by a directed flow of fluid in the mitochondrion.

questions.stem: Lipase catalyses the hydrolysis of triglycerides but has no effect on starch. What is the reason?

options.text: Starch molecules are too large to enter the active site, but any molecule smaller than starch could.
The active site of lipase is complementary in shape and chemical properties to a triglyceride only.
Starch requires more energy to break down than lipase is able to supply to the reaction.
Lipase seeks out triglyceride molecules in the fluid and ignores starch molecules it meets.

questions.stem: At high substrate concentrations, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction levels off even when more substrate is added. Why?

options.text: Every active site is occupied almost all the time, so extra substrate finds no free site to bind.
The enzyme molecules have been used up by the reaction, so no more product can be formed.
The high concentration of substrate denatures the enzyme, so its active site stops working.
The amount of energy the enzyme can supply each second has reached its upper limit.

questions.stem: Illustrative data. Catalase was added to hydrogen peroxide and the volume of oxygen collected was recorded: 0 s, 0 cm³; 20 s, 12 cm³; 40 s, 20 cm³; 60 s, 24 cm³. What is the initial rate of reaction?

options.text: 0.40 cm³ s⁻¹
1.7 s per cm³
20 cm³ in 40 s
0.6 cm³ s⁻¹

questions.explanation: The initial rate is the gradient of the first, steepest part of the graph: 12 cm³ of oxygen in the first 20 s gives 12 / 20 = 0.6 cm³ s⁻¹.

questions.stem: How does an enzyme affect the energy changes of the reaction it catalyses?

options.text: It lowers the energy of the products, so that more energy is released overall than would be without the enzyme.
It lowers the activation energy but leaves the energy difference between substrate and products unchanged.
It supplies the activation energy, transferring its own energy to the substrate to break the bonds.
It releases energy by breaking bonds in the substrate, and this provides the activation energy.

questions.stem: Catalase in liver cells increases the rate at which hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen by a factor of many millions. What is the benefit to the cell of this increase in rate?

options.text: Hydrogen peroxide could not be broken down at all without an enzyme to make it possible.
Toxic hydrogen peroxide is removed fast enough at cell temperature to prevent damage.
Catalase supplies the energy that the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide needs.
The reaction releases energy that the cell captures as ATP, as in respiration.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes metabolism in a living organism?

options.text: The set of reactions that release energy from food molecules to keep the organism alive and active.
A series of reactions whose rate is set only by how much substrate the organism takes in from outside.
A network of interdependent enzyme-catalysed reactions, each controlled through its own enzyme.
A set of reactions catalysed by a few general-purpose enzymes that act on many substrates.

questions.stem: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?

options.text: Its peptide bonds are broken, so the polypeptide chain splits into its separate amino acids.
Its shape alters only briefly and then returns to normal once the conditions are restored.
Its three-dimensional structure changes, so the active site no longer fits the substrate.
It is killed, because enzymes are living particles that are destroyed by heat or acid.
